reasoning: The underlying problem — that non-substantive verbosity raises an LLM judge's approval of fixed-quality (including incorrect) answers — is extensively documented. Verbosity/length bias is quantified (LLM +17.3% vs human +12.9% preference for longer responses; judges favor "lower quality and less persuasive" longer arguments) in arXiv 2310.10076 and 2407.01085, and the exact methodology of holding content constant while varying length to detect "length-driven preference flips via targeted length interventions" already exists (2407.01085, 2511.12573). The specific flip-incorrect-to-PASS angle is directly studied by AdvJudge-Zero (arXiv 2512.17375), which appends padding/control tokens to flip "No" to "Yes" with high false-positive rates on math/reasoning judges, and reward-hacking work shows appending phrases like "Solution" or a colon inflates judge scores regardless of correctness. Even the dose-response shape (bias growing with length difference, stable 40-100 words, declining beyond) is already characterized. The proposal's only mild differentiators are the factual-QA PASS/FAIL framing on small open judges plus per-judge curve fitting — minor recombinations of established findings rather than an unexplored contribution.

evidence.title: Verbosity Bias in Preference Labeling by Large Language Models (2310.10076)
evidence.summary: Establishes that LLM judges systematically prefer more verbose responses; foundational documentation of the verbosity-bias problem the proposal targets.

evidence.title: Explaining Length Bias in LLM-Based Preference Evaluations (2407.01085)
evidence.summary: Uses the exact controlled methodology the proposal proposes — holding content constant while varying length, applying targeted length interventions to identify length-driven preference flips — and characterizes the dose-response shape (bias grows with size difference, stable 40-100 words, declines >100).

evidence.title: AdvJudge-Zero: Binary Decision Flips in LLM-as-a-Judge via Adversarial Control Tokens (2512.17375)
evidence.summary: Directly studies flipping incorrect answers to PASS in a judge: appended low-perplexity tokens flip 'No' to 'Yes', causing high false-positive rates when open/specialized judges score incorrect math and reasoning answers — very close to the proposal's flip-via-padding question.

evidence.title: Mitigating Length Bias in RLHF through a Causal Lens (2511.12573)
evidence.summary: Counterfactual augmentation generating response variants by manipulating length while keeping semantic content constant, then identifying length-driven preference flips — the same hold-claim-fixed/vary-padding design.

evidence.title: Is LLM-as-a-Judge Robust? Universal Adversarial Attacks on Zero-shot LLM Assessment (2402.14016)
evidence.summary: Short universal adversarial phrases concatenated to answers inflate judge scores, with absolute scoring more susceptible than comparative — supports that appended non-substantive text raises pass/score for fixed content.

evidence.title: Reward hacking via LLM-judge exploits (verbosity, appended phrases)
evidence.summary: Documents that appending short phrases like 'Solution' or a single colon causes LLM judges to assign high scores regardless of answer quality, framing verbosity/padding as a known reward-hacking and oversight-bypass channel.
